proof_nl:
Let N(q) = product_{i=1}^m (q^(b+d+i) - 1) and D(q) = product_{i=1}^m (q^(b+i) - 1). For each i, (1 - q^(b+d+i)) / (1 - q^(b+i)) = (q^(b+d+i) - 1) / (q^(b+i) - 1), so F_{b,m,d}(q) = N(q) / D(q).

I first prove that D divides N in C[q]. Take any complex root zeta of D. Then zeta^(b+i) = 1 for some i in {1, ..., m}, so zeta is a root of unity. Let t be the exact order of zeta. For any positive integer r, zeta is a root of q^r - 1 if and only if t divides r, and in that case the root is simple because the derivative of q^r - 1 is r q^(r-1), which is nonzero at zeta.

Therefore the multiplicity of zeta as a root of D is exactly the number of indices i in {1, ..., m} such that t divides b+i. That number is the number of multiples of t in the interval {b+1, ..., b+m}, namely
floor((b+m)/t) - floor(b/t).
Similarly, the multiplicity of zeta as a root of N is the number of multiples of t in {b+d+1, ..., b+d+m}, namely
floor((b+d+m)/t) - floor((b+d)/t).
By the hypothesis of the lemma, for every positive integer t we have
floor((b+m)/t) - floor(b/t) <= floor((b+d+m)/t) - floor((b+d)/t),
so the multiplicity of zeta in N is at least its multiplicity in D.

Since this holds for every complex root zeta of D, every root of D occurs in N with at least the same multiplicity. Hence D divides N in C[q]. Now D is monic and N belongs to Z[q]. Perform polynomial division in Z[q]: there exist Q(q), R(q) in Z[q] with
N(q) = D(q) Q(q) + R(q),   deg R < deg D.
But over C[q] we already know that D divides N, so the remainder must be 0. Thus R = 0 and Q = N/D = F_{b,m,d}. Therefore F_{b,m,d}(q) lies in Z[q].

Now set n = b+d+m, k = b+m, and l = b. Because b >= 0, m >= 0, and d >= m, we have 0 <= l <= k <= n, hence 0 <= k,l <= n. Using the standard product definition of the Gaussian binomial coefficient,
[n choose k]_q = product_{i=1}^k (1 - q^(n-k+i)) / (1 - q^i),
we get
[n choose b+m]_q = product_{i=1}^{b+m} (1 - q^(d+i)) / (1 - q^i)
and
[n choose b]_q = product_{i=1}^b (1 - q^(d+m+i)) / (1 - q^i).
Taking the ratio and cancelling the common factors with i = 1, ..., b gives
[n choose b+m]_q / [n choose b]_q
= product_{i=b+1}^{b+m} (1 - q^(d+i)) / (1 - q^i)
= product_{j=1}^m (1 - q^(b+d+j)) / (1 - q^(b+j))
= F_{b,m,d}(q).
So F_{b,m,d}(q) is a quotient of two Gaussian binomial coefficients with the same top parameter n, and we have already proved that this quotient is a polynomial in q.

By the allowed root semantic sketch, whenever 0 <= k,l <= n and [n choose k]_q / [n choose l]_q is a polynomial in q, all of its coefficients are nonnegative. Applying that statement with n = b+d+m, k = b+m, and l = b, we conclude that every coefficient of F_{b,m,d}(q) is nonnegative. Since F_{b,m,d}(q) is already in Z[q], these coefficients are nonnegative integers.

Hence F_{b,m,d}(q) lies in Z[q], and every coefficient in its standard expansion is a nonnegative integer, exactly as claimed.
solver_summary: Write F as N(q)/D(q) with N(q) = product_{i=1}^m (q^(b+d+i)-1) and D(q) = product_{i=1}^m (q^(b+i)-1). For a root zeta of D of order t, its multiplicity in D is floor((b+m)/t)-floor(b/t), while its multiplicity in N is floor((b+d+m)/t)-floor((b+d)/t). The assumed floor inequality therefore shows that every root of D appears in N with at least the same multiplicity, so D divides N and F belongs to Z[q]. Then set n=b+d+m, k=b+m, l=b and check directly from the product formula that F = [n choose k]_q / [n choose l]_q. The allowed root semantic sketch then gives nonnegativity of all coefficients.
vetter_reason: The divisibility/polynomiality part is largely sound, but the key identification of F with a Gaussian-binomial quotient is wrong for the chosen n, and the nonnegativity conclusion is obtained only by citing a forbidden ancestor-equivalent root claim. The lemma still looks salvageable with a rewritten proof.
